2.definition: Modeled on the institutions and forms of industrialized Europe and America. The Western powers demanded that Japan adopt Western-style law, government, and armed forces before they would revise the unequal treaties, and Meiji reformers set out to copy the templates they judged most suitable — chiefly Prussian ones.

4.definition: The French silk engineer hired by the Meiji finance ministry to design and run the Tomioka Silk Mill (opened 1872), Japan's flagship pilot factory for Western mechanical silk-reeling.
A Kobe-based trading house that grew into one of Meiji and Taisho Japan's largest commercial conglomerates before collapsing in the 1927 financial crisis.
Japan's first railway, an 18-mile line opened in 1872 linking the capital, Tokyo, to the treaty port of Yokohama. It became the seed of the national rail network.

5.definition: The 1885 reform that scrapped the old Council of State (Dajōkan) and replaced it with a European-style cabinet of ministers — each running a department, all answering to a prime minister. Itō Hirobumi took the first prime minister's chair that December.

An 1886 decree that turned Tokyo's university into the elite forge for the new bureaucratic civil service, with sister imperial universities later sprouting in Kyoto, Kyushu, and elsewhere to staff the modern state.

The bedrock principle of the Meiji Constitution: all sovereign power flowed from the emperor, who held legislative, executive, and judicial authority and from whose grant the constitution itself was said to derive — the opposite of constitutions a people grant themselves.

The Meiji franchise as designed: only adult men paying at least 15 yen a year in direct national taxes could vote — about 1% of the population, some 450,000 people — a property bar tilted toward landlords and the commercial class, widened only gradually before becoming universal for men in 1925.

The constitutional fault line by which the army and navy reported straight to the emperor, outside cabinet control — the so-called 'right of supreme command' (tōsuiken) that let the military set its own course and would prove catastrophic in the 1930s.
Modeled on contemporary Europe and America — the Western forms (dress, architecture, law, industry, military drill) Meiji Japan deliberately adopted to modernize.

6.definition: The Shinto fanatic who assassinated education minister Mori Arinori on February 11, 1889 — the day the Meiji Constitution was promulgated — convinced that Mori had defiled the Ise Shrine. His act fused the two streams of Meiji ideological formation: a schoolroom literacy that let him write his manifesto, and a sacred-nationalist fervor that drove him to kill over a perceived insult to a curtain.

Japan's first state institution for Western classical music, founded in Tokyo in 1887 to train musicians and music teachers for the new education system. It was the channel through which European orchestral and operatic traditions entered Japan, and in 1949 it merged into what is now the Tokyo University of the Arts.
Modeled on contemporary Europe and America — the Western forms (dress, architecture, law, industry, military drill) Meiji Japan deliberately adopted to modernize.

7.definition: A Japanese rallying phrase — literally "lying on firewood and tasting bile" — meaning to endure hardship while nursing a long-term resolve for revenge. It became a national slogan after the 1895 Triple Intervention forced Japan to give back the Liaodong Peninsula, channeling public humiliation into a decade of military buildup aimed at Russia.

Anti-colonial activists in French-ruled Vietnam who, like nationalists across colonized Asia, seized on Japan's 1905 defeat of Russia as proof that a non-Western people could modernize and beat a European empire on its own terms.
Early independence-minded reformers in the Dutch East Indies who took Japan's victory over Russia as evidence that European colonial dominance was not permanent or racially destined.
Independence advocates in the Philippines — recently passed from Spanish to American rule — who pointed to Japan's rise as a model of successful Asian self-strengthening against Western powers.

8.definition: The imperial tomb at Fushimi-Momoyama, south of Kyoto, where Emperor Meiji was buried in 1912 — on the grounds of the old Fushimi Castle of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, deliberately reviving classical imperial burial near the ancient capital rather than in Tokyo.
The wife of General Nogi Maresuke, who agreed to die alongside him; on the night of the Meiji Emperor's funeral in 1912 she cut her own throat with a dagger as her husband committed seppuku.
Of Vietnam — here the early Vietnamese nationalists who looked to Meiji Japan as the model of an Asian nation that modernized and resisted Western domination.
